extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, literary critics, and readers of English dramatic and poetic criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and critical criteria for judging and composing English poetry and stage plays — covering language, wit, plotting, character, prosody, borrowing, and the influence of contemporary conversation/audience. Focused on qualities that mark a refined age of letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refinement of an age
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement of our Wit, Language and Conversation; or, an alteration in them for the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden sets as the overarching criterion that a refined age shows measurable improvement in wit, language, and conversation. He proposes to demonstrate that the present age's language, wit, and conversation are improved and refined above the last, and that our plays have thereby received advantages. Use this threefold axis (wit, language, conversation) to judge literary progress between ages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language refinement: reject improper old forms or admit better new ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Refinement of a language consists either in rejecting such old words, or phrases, which are ill sounding, or improper; or in admitting new, which are more proper, more sounding, and more significant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two permitted movements: (1) excise antiquated/ill-sounding/improper words and phrases; (2) adopt new words/phrases that are more proper or sonorous. Distinguish accidental loss-by-custom from improvement: only rejection of words that are actually improper counts as refinement. Examples: many modern admissions enrich the tongue; some imports are ornamental; poets have also 'applied received words to a new signification' as legitimate refinement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness of language (grammar, syntax, diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid solecisms of speech and notorious flaws in sense — grammatical errors, false constructions, misplaced prepositions, redundant pronouns, and improper concord or articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden provides many concrete anti-patterns (e.g., Jonson's misplaced preposition at line end, redundant 'they', false syntax like 'his' with 'heaven', improper comparative constructions). He argues that such errors are common in earlier masters and that present writers should be more correct. When evaluating, look for clear solecisms, false constructions, redundant or antiquated particles that obscure sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prosody and euphony: well-placing of words
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-placing of words, for the sweetness of pronunciation, is an element of refinement (Waller introduced it).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Word order should favour sweet pronunciation and natural cadence. Avoid constructions that sacrifice euphony or place prepositions and particles awkwardly (e.g., preposition stranded at mid-period). This is especially important in tragedy, which 'ought to be more high and sounding than any other kind of poetry.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of register to genre
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy ought to be more high and sounding than any other kind of poetry; meanness of expression is improper in tragedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match diction and expression to the dignity of the subject. Examples: lines in Catiline showing 'be' for 'are' or mean expressions are unacceptable in tragedy. Assess whether the language and tone suit the genre's expectations (e.g., elevated diction for tragedy, courtly polish for comedy aimed at gentry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plotting and decorum of the stage
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct plotting — coherent, probable, decorous action appropriate to the stage — is essential; avoid ridiculous incoherent stories or impossibilities which displace the dependence of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden criticises older plots as 'lame' or 'ridiculous incoherent story' (citing Pericles, Winter's Tale, Love's Labour Lost, Measure for Measure). A good plot should show unity, plausible motivation, decorum (proper conduct for characters and situations), and a sensible economy of incidents so scenes do not dominate 'the business of an age.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice and maintenance of characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Select characters with judgement and maintain what has been chosen to the end: characters should be consistently drawn and preserved throughout the play.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jonson is praised for choice of characters and maintaining them; faults occur when characters behave inconsistently (e.g., sudden comic interruptions that undermine a hero's serious scene). Evaluate whether characters remain coherent in temperament, social standing, and speech, and whether their presence supports the plot without jarring shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness and steadiness of wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit must suit the dignity of the subject and the character: avoid precipitous falls from high thought to low expression; avoid redundant or groveling 'clenches' and humour that is merely meanness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden faults Shakespeare for turning from great thought to low expression and Fletcher for redundancy and loss of judgement mid-play ('if he pleases you in the first three acts, he is frequently so tired...'). Judge wit by its appropriateness (is it 'gentlemanly' when required?), steadiness across scenes, and whether it enhances character rather than merely exhibiting cleverness or vulgarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicious borrowing vs. corruption by foreign idiom
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not corrupt English idiom by mixing it too much with French; judicious adoption is fine, but turning English into French is a sophistication, not an improvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique fashion-driven importation of foreign phrases; favour measured borrowing where the new term fills a lack ('we have admitted many [words] which we wanted'), but condemn affectation where travellers or fops substitute French merely as fashion. Evaluate whether foreign terms enrich or displace the native idiom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive grafting: applying words to new signification
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying received words to a new signification (grafting on old words) is a legitimate method of beautifying the language and refining it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden endorses Horace's notion of novel effect produced by dextrous collocation ('Dixeris egregie, notum si callida verbum Reddiderit junctura novum'). Assess creative tropes and metaphors that heighten significance without violating sense or idiom; this counts as refinement rather than corruption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience and social conversation as a source of refinement
rubrics_metrics.description: Refinement in writing is derived from the refinement of conversation and the example of courtly manners; writers profit by being conversant with polished society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden insists that the court and the king's example made conversation more free and gallant, which enriched comedy and manners onstage. When evaluating, consider the intended audience and whether the play reflects and benefits from contemporary social manners (gallantry, civility) — i.e., whether it engages the cultivated judgement of its audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of criticism in improving wit
rubrics_metrics.description: A severe critic is the greatest help to a good wit: criticism keeps a poet within bounds and aids correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden argues that observing and censuring faults is a step toward correction; value informed criticism that identifies solecisms and faults. When composing, expect and use critical scrutiny to refine language and plotting rather than seeing it as mere hostility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy: social refinement of characters and humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy should entertain refined company by exposing follies of gentility and conversation rather than dwelling on coarse rags-and-tankard clownishness; love and gallantry are important foundations in comedy for many other languages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dryden contrasts Jonson's low, clownish humour with a newer courtly comedy that pleases gentlemen. Evaluate comic scenes for whether they reflect the manners and raillery of the intended social class; avoid overreliance on low buffoonery when addressing a refined audience.
